title: Trump Expresses Regret Over Supreme Court Appointments, Citing Unfavorable Rulings
snippet: In a recent interview, Donald Trump voiced frustration with Justices Gorsuch, Kavanaugh, and Barrett, saying he regrets appointing them after they voted against his policies.
content:
Former President Donald Trump publicly admitted in a newly published interview that he regrets nominating Supreme Court Justices Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh, and Amy Coney Barrett, venting frustration over several major legal rulings that went against his interests.

Speaking with Time Magazine, the former president lamented that the three conservative justices he appointed have repeatedly broken with his positions on critical cases. When asked directly if he regretted their appointments, Trump responded, "Yeah. Yeah. What can I do? I put them in. They voted against me too often. I gave them the position of a lifetime, and they vote against me often."

Tensions Over Major Court Rulings

Trump’s three judicial selections during his administration established a 6-3 conservative supermajority, steering the nation's highest court markedly to the right on numerous constitutional issues. Despite this ideological shift, the justices have frequently demonstrated judicial independence in cases directly affecting Trump's policy agenda.

The former president reserved sharp criticism for a February ruling that struck down his sweeping global tariffs, which the court determined were unlawfully implemented under national emergency powers. Justices Gorsuch and Barrett notably joined the majority in that 6-3 decision. Trump was also angered by the high court's refusal to reinstate a Postal Service restriction on mail-in ballots, later asserting on Truth Social that the appointees were "merely a shell of their original selves."

Questions of Judicial Loyalty

When pressed on what he expects from Supreme Court nominees, Trump acknowledged a preference for loyalty while insisting he prioritizes judicial outcomes. "I do like loyalty, yeah," Trump told the interviewer, before clarifying, "No, I don't want loyalty. I want good decisions."
